one_liner: Book example: a scope guard templated on its cleanup lambda, removing std::function type erasure and its per-guard overhead.
what_it_does: ScopeGuard<Callable> runs a cleanup callable when the scope ends unless commit() was called; it is created with MakeGuard([&]{ ... }) and held in an auto variable. The baseline in the same file is a non-template ScopeGuard that stores the cleanup in a std::function<void()>. Other Chapter 11 files build ON_SCOPE_EXIT, ON_SCOPE_SUCCESS and ON_SCOPE_FAILURE macros on the same template design, using std::uncaught_exceptions in C++17.
how_it_is_fast: The callable's type is a template parameter and the lambda is stored by value, so the destructor calls it directly and the compiler inlines it: no std::function construction, no manager/invoker function pointers and no indirect call. In a reduced copy compiled to assembly by the enricher (GCC 13.3 and Clang 18, -O2 and -O3), the template-guard loop compiled to the same code as the hand-written explicit delete, while the std::function guard kept an indirect call through its invoker.
when_to_use: Rollback or cleanup (delete, close, undo) in functions with several return paths or exceptions, where the cleanup is a short lambda over locals.
Hot paths that create a guard per call or per iteration, where std::function setup and an indirect call (about 1.8 ns per guard in the book's run, derived from the relayed numbers) show up.
Local guards that can be declared with auto, which is the normal way scope guards are used.
C++17 code that also wants success-only or failure-only cleanup: the chapter's ON_SCOPE_SUCCESS and ON_SCOPE_FAILURE macros use the same template approach.
when_not_to_use: Guards that must share one type: stored as a class member, in a container or returned through a non-template interface; that needs type erasure (std::function or the buffer-based sibling).
When a maintained guard is already available: Boost.ScopeExit, folly::ScopeGuard and std::experimental::scope_exit use the same template design.
Cleanup code that can throw: the destructor is implicitly noexcept, so a throwing cleanup calls std::terminate.
Expecting the book's 2.9x delete-case gain in real code: the clean comparison is about 1.8 ns per guard, negligible next to I/O or allocation in the guarded scope.

integration.dependencies: none for the guard itself (it needs <utility> for std::exchange, which the file only gets through benchmark/benchmark.h; with <functional> alone GCC 13 libstdc++ rejects std::exchange). The benchmark needs Google Benchmark; there are no build files, and unmerged third-party PR #11 adds a Chapter11 CMakeLists.txt (C++20, benchmark v1.7.1, no build type or flags).
integration.min_toolchain: C++14 (std::exchange); enricher compiled a reduced copy with GCC 13.3 and Clang 18 at -std=c++17. The ON_SCOPE_SUCCESS/FAILURE variants need C++17 (std::uncaught_exceptions).
integration.thread_safety: not documented; a guard is a local object used by one thread, and the captured state's safety is up to the caller
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same construct/commit/run-at-exit behaviour, but the guard's type depends on the lambda, so it is declared with auto via MakeGuard and cannot replace the std::function guard where a single named type is needed

gotchas: Benchmark defect in the delete case: in a reduced copy compiled to assembly (GCC 13.3, Clang 18, -O2/-O3), both compilers removed the new int(42)/delete pair entirely from the explicit and template rows (only the rand() call remains), while the std::function and buffer-guard rows keep operator new and the indirect delete. The 13.4 ns against 4.56 ns (2.9x) row therefore compares a real allocation against none; use the nodelete row.

MakeGuard with a named (lvalue) lambda does not compile: Callable deduces to a reference, the two constructors collapse to one signature (GCC 13.3: 'cannot be overloaded'; Clang 18: 'multiple overloads of ScopeGuard instantiate to the same signature'). Pass the lambda inline or std::move it.
The plain guard fires on every exit, success included, until commit() is called (checked on a reduced copy: commit() disarms it); use the chapter's ON_SCOPE_FAILURE variant for failure-only rollback.

Do not copy the file's ScopeGuardTypeErasedFast class alongside it: it redeclares mutable bool commit_, shadowing the base flag, so commit() never disarms it and a moved-from guard still fires (reduced copy: cleanup ran once after commit(), twice after a move).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Against the catalogued inline-buffer type-erased guard from the same chapter, this one is as fast as hand-written cleanup, has no size or trivially-copyable limits on the lambda, and does not have that class's commit() bug; take the buffer guard only when one non-template guard type is required (after fixing it). The other catalogued utilities are unrelated.
verified_claims_summary: The book reports (relayed by the seed lead; the repo holds only the Google Benchmark source) template guard 4.50 ns against 6.29 ns for the std::function guard with explicit code at 4.48 ns when no delete happens, and 4.56 ns against 13.4 ns (explicit 4.54 ns) when an int is allocated and deleted each iteration; compiler, flags and CPU are not stated, and every row except noop includes a rand() call, which is most of the 4.5 ns. Because only the std::function row pays a real new/delete in the delete case, subtracting its own nodelete-to-delete step (7.1 ns) leaves about 1.7 ns of guard overhead, matching the nodelete gap of about 1.8 ns, roughly 1.4x on this rand()-dominated loop (derived from the relayed numbers).
status_note: Stale Packt companion repo (last commit 2024-08-29; CMake PR #11 for Chapter11 unmerged since 2023-01-23), MIT; the guard is about 30 lines, so copy it with an explicit #include <utility>, or use a maintained library guard.
